request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]

Age: 21

Gender: Male

Admission Date: [redacted]

Discharge Date: [redacted]
Discharge Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course: 

Patient presented with acute onset of left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath after using an E-cigarette during his break at work, which he had been using for the past 3 years. A chest X-ray at an urgent care center revealed a small left-sided pneumothorax, which progressed to a moderate sized pneumothorax as seen on a repeat chest X-ray in the ED. A left-sided chest tube was inserted, which successfully resolved his pneumothorax. CT chest was obtained and revealed left-sided atelectasis. 

The patient remained stable throughout his hospital course and was discharged home on hospital day 3 with instructions to avoid vaping. He was advised to follow up with his primary care physician for further evaluation and management, and to seek medical attention if he experienced any recurrence of his symptoms.

Discharge Medications: None

Discharge Instructions: The patient was advised to avoid vaping and to follow up with his primary care physician for further evaluation and management. 

Follow-up: The patient was instructed to follow up with his primary care physician within the next 1-2 weeks for further evaluation and management.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode is a pneumothorax in a 21-year-old man with no trauma and no known underlying lung disease, so it is best classed as a spontaneous pneumothorax. The vaping history is a possible trigger, but the pneumothorax itself was the condition treated, with a chest tube.

In ICD-10-AM, spontaneous pneumothorax is coded to J93. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax falls under J93.1, which is within the J93 category. Another option is U07.0, vaping-related disorder, which exists in ICD-10-CM. It is not a chapter-style category in ICD-10-AM, and it would be used with a manifestation code anyway. The atelectasis (J98.1) is a CT finding and not the main reason for admission.

CODE: J93
